title: Honey from many trees
hookLine: bees gather from many trees, and the honey cannot say whose
carry: one self in all, and each still itself
tomorrow: two rivers run opposite ways. where do they both end up?
last: THE BIRD SETTLES WHERE IT'S TIED.

cards: The group project comes back with one grade. Somebody made the slides, somebody did the research, somebody stayed up fixing the ending. Now it's one thing, and it's hard to say whose sentence is whose.
Honey works the same way. Ask a single drop which flower it came from, and there's no answer to give. That's the picture Uddalaka hands his son next.

teach.b: Bees make honey, the father says, by gathering the juices of many kinds of trees and bringing them to one. In the honey, those juices can't tell themselves apart.

teach.h: NO DROP SAYS: I'M FROM THAT TREE.
teach.b: None can say, I'm the juice of that tree, I'm the juice of this one. In the same way, all these creatures, when they merge into Being, don't know that they have merged. Then a line that keeps the picture honest.
Whatever they are here, a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, a worm, a moth, a gnat, a mosquito, that they become again. So the honey isn't everything blurring into mush.

teach.h: THE TIGER IS STILL A TIGER.
teach.b: The tiger comes back a tiger, the gnat a gnat.
What the bees show is something underneath the differences: a sweetness all of them share and no one of them owns.
Hindu teachers call it the one atman in every creature, and many Hindus explain namaste, palms together, as a bow to the divine in the other person. Then the refrain again.
That which is the finest essence, this whole world has that as its self. That is the real. That is the self.
That you are, Shvetaketu. And again the son says: teach me more. Hold that next to the group project.
The finished thing belongs to everyone and to no one alone, and the people who made it stay exactly who they are.

how: In Vedanta study, the honey, the rivers, the tree and the other pictures of Chandogya 6 are read one by one, each closing on the refrain tat tvam asi.

o: that you are: one essence under many lives
that is the honey you must go and gather
you're a part, so your own self doesn't count

games.q: the bees and the honey. tap the pairs.

s: the honey passage is only a nature lesson about bees
it's a picture: so all creatures, merged in Being, don't know they have merged.
in the honey, the juices can't say which tree they came from
none can say: I'm the juice of that tree, I'm the juice of this one.

games.q: a friend says: if everything shares one essence, then nobody is really different and personalities don't matter. what does the honey passage say?
o: the differences stay: the tiger comes back a tiger, the gnat a gnat.
right: in the honey, every difference is gone for good.
only humans share the essence; animals are left out.
games.why: whatever they are here, tiger, lion, wolf, gnat, that they become again. one sweetness underneath, and the tiger still a tiger.

practice: Bring to mind the hands behind one thing you ate or used today: who grew it, carried it, cooked it, sold it. For each face, fold your hands at your heart, or just bow inside, and say namaste.
Each one exactly who they are, one self in all.

wordCard.voice: Tat tvam asi: that you are. In the honey, the juices of many trees become one, and the father says it again.

orig.note: Sanskrit: honey. The father's picture for one essence beneath many beings.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: one self in all, and every tiger still a tiger. Day 1755, done.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.9.1–4 (as bees make honey by gathering the juices of many trees and bringing them to one, and the juices cannot tell 'I am the juice of this tree, of that tree', so all creatures merged in Being do not know they have merged; whatever they are here, tiger, lion, wolf, boar, worm, moth, gnat, mosquito, that they become again; that which is the finest essence ... that you are, Shvetaketu; please, sir, teach me more)
